title: Turn dining ideas into a brief that is personal to you
intro: A dining gallery can help you recognise the style you enjoy before you have the words for it. You may be drawn to a relaxed sharing table, a carefully plated main course or a warm setting for two. Use the collection to identify those details and then connect them with your own occasion. The guide below explains how to translate visual preferences into a practical menu and service brief, with the date, property and guest experience shaping what can be arranged.

sections.title: Choose a few details, then make them your own
paragraphs: Save the elements that matter most: the serving style, the balance of dishes or the mood of the table. Tell us why you like them. That is more useful than asking for an exact recreation without knowing the ingredients, equipment or setting behind an image.

We can then discuss how a suitable version would work for your guests and budget. Photographs identified as previous myCHEF work show the particular service described; other dining ideas help start the conversation. Your own menu, staffing and presentation are confirmed in the proposal for your booking.

sections.title: Use photographs to describe the details you like
paragraphs: A photograph is a useful starting point for a brief when you can explain what attracts you to it. It might be the way dishes are shared, the restrained table styling, the colour of the food or the relaxed setting. Choose a few details rather than asking the team to recreate every object in an image without knowing the venue or budget.

Then connect those preferences to your own occasion. How many people will attend? Is the meal indoors or outside? What equipment and table space are available? A visual direction becomes a workable plan only when it is translated into a menu, staffing and a list of items that can be confirmed for your booking.

Where photographs are identified as previous myCHEF work, use them to understand the documented setting and service shown. They do not automatically define what every package includes. Your proposal remains the reference for the food, presentation and hospitality that will be arranged for your own date and location.

sections.title: Match the service to the way your guests gather
paragraphs: Some occasions revolve around conversation at one table; others work better when guests move around and eat at their own pace. Describe how you imagine the gathering before choosing individual dishes. Food that is comfortable to eat standing may need different portions and presentation from a meal designed for a seated place setting.

Sharing service can encourage conversation, while plated courses create a more defined sequence. A mixed format may begin with small bites and move to a seated main course. Each option has implications for staff, crockery and the kitchen, so discuss the complete flow rather than deciding the menu and service separately.

Think about the guests who may need a quieter seat, an earlier meal or a simple alternative. A considerate arrangement makes them part of the occasion without requiring a complicated last-minute change. Once the format is clear, the chef can recommend dishes that suit it and the team can price the practical support needed.

link.label: Discuss the style of your occasion

sections.title: Make the table work as well as it looks
paragraphs: A beautiful table should still leave room to eat comfortably. Consider the number of plates, glasses and serving dishes before deciding on flowers or decorative pieces. A sharing menu needs space in the centre; a plated menu may need room for several pieces of cutlery or a separate bread plate. The menu and table layout should be planned together.

Check what is available at the property and what needs to be arranged. Crockery, serving platters, linen and glassware are not interchangeable with kitchen equipment, and they should not be assumed to be included unless your proposal says so. Tell the team if you want a particular style, colour palette or level of formality.

Lighting and access matter, too. Guests need to see the food, and staff need a safe route between the table and kitchen. A simple, thoughtfully arranged setting can feel more welcoming than an overcrowded display. Confirm setup and clear-down responsibilities so the presentation remains practical throughout the occasion.

link.label: Discuss your table and service requirements

sections.title: Choose courses that belong together
paragraphs: A memorable dinner menu is more than a list of favourite dishes. Think about how the courses follow one another: a fresh beginning, a satisfying main course and a finish that complements what came before. Repeating the same rich ingredient or cooking style throughout can make a meal feel heavier than intended, even when each dish is good on its own.

Share your must-have dishes and let the chef recommend the supporting courses. If a particular main course is the centrepiece, the starter and dessert can be chosen to balance it. The menu should also respect the kitchen and service team, especially when several plates need to reach the table together.

Consider the pace you want. A relaxed family gathering, a birthday dinner and an interactive tasting menu may all use different course structures. Agreeing the format early makes it easier to discuss portions, staffing and timing. The most persuasive menu is one that sounds enjoyable to your guests and can be delivered comfortably in the setting.

sections.title: Look beyond the finished table when reviewing previous work
paragraphs: The finished setting is only one part of an occasion. When reviewing a previous service, look at how the food was presented, how guests could reach it and how the setup suited the venue. A compact yacht table, a villa dining room and a larger reception each call for different decisions, even when the overall style feels similar.

Use documented examples to ask practical questions about your own brief. Would the same format work with your guest count? Does your venue have comparable preparation space? Would additional staff be needed to serve the dishes in the way you want? These questions turn a portfolio into a useful planning tool rather than a collection of attractive images.

A previous booking is not a fixed package or a promise of identical availability. Menus, seasonal ingredients, staffing and equipment need to be reviewed for each occasion. Share the elements you like, and the team can explain how a suitable version could be planned around your date, property and expectations.

sections.title: Send a brief that makes the first proposal useful
paragraphs: A useful enquiry can be short and still contain the essentials. Include your Dubai location, preferred date or start date, number of people, the meals you need and any essential dietary requirements. Add whether the service is a recurring household arrangement or a one-off occasion, because those lead to different menus, staffing and pricing discussions.

Then describe what a successful result would feel like. Perhaps you want dinner ready when you arrive home, a fridge organised for several busy days or a celebration where you can stay with your guests. This helps the team recommend a suitable format instead of making you choose from options that do not address your main priority.

If you have a budget in mind, share it with the scope. That creates a practical starting point for discussing the number of courses, frequency or staffing. An enquiry begins a conversation; the final menu, availability, responsibilities and price are confirmed in the written booking details.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
cta.label: Discuss my requirements
